aAbout: God's Eye View is an open-source 3D world globe simulator — 'a spy-satellite simulator in your browser, except the data is real.' It renders Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles through Cesium and layers live aircraft, ships, satellites, earthquakes, traffic and public cameras from open sources, all processed locally in your browser. It went viral in 2026 for its voice-controlled AI agent, cockpit view and sensor-style visual modes. It is software you run yourself — via Pinokio one-click, a terminal install, or Docker — not a website you open.

aLink.label: WorldEye: the God's Eye View alternative

aStrengths: God's Eye View is the live and ownable tool: a photorealistic 3D globe layered with aircraft, ships, satellites, earthquakes and cameras happening now, plus cockpit view, 3D aircraft models, sensor looks (FLIR, night vision) and a scene director for cinematic tours — all free, all running on your machine with data you can inspect, extend and keep. Its voice agent genuinely has no equivalent here: you talk to the globe and it flies, tracks and annotates. For creators, tinkerers and anyone who wants the present-tense planet, nothing archival matches it.
bAbout: Google Earth is the world's most detailed free virtual globe: high-resolution satellite and aerial imagery, 3D cities and terrain, Street View at ground level, a historical-imagery archive reaching back decades, and tools for measuring, drawing and telling stories with places (including guided Voyager tours and Google Earth Studio for animations). Google Earth Pro — once $399/year — has been free since 2015. Everything in it is archival: the imagery shows the world as it was photographed, not as it is now.
bStrengths: Google Earth is the gold standard for exploring a place: the most detailed 3D cities anywhere, Street View, the deepest historical imagery archive (decades back), powerful measurement and drawing tools, KML/KMZ data import and Earth Studio for cinematic animations — all permanently free. Nobody matches its imagery depth, 3D building coverage and the familiarity billions of users already have. For deep place exploration, its scale is untouchable.
betterAnswer: They solve different problems. God's Eye View is a free, open-source 3D globe you run on your own computer — unmatched for live data, voice control and hackability, with a modest camera layer (~4,000) and no imagery archive. Google Earth is a hosted explorer built around place depth: the deepest archival imagery, 3D cities and Street View, completely free and instantly open, with nothing live at all. If you want to watch the planet move, install God's Eye View; if you want to explore how a place looks and looked, open Google Earth.
consA: You must install and run it yourself (Pinokio, terminal or Docker)
Camera layer is small (~4,000) beside hosted atlases
Ships need a free third-party key; voice spends your OpenAI credit
No general history archive — it shows the present, not past decades
No recording, no alerts, no hosted sharing for a team
consB: Imagery is archival — days to years old, never live
No live flights, ships or cameras of any kind
Weather is limited to a real-time cloud layer
No live event tracking for fires, storms or earthquakes

faqs.a: No — they are unrelated products. God's Eye View is free open-source software by Bilawal Sidhu and Sameh Khamis that you install and run locally. Google Earth is Google's hosted virtual globe. They share a genre — 3D earth explorers — and little else.
faqs.q: Is God's Eye View the same as Google Earth?

faqs.a: Yes. The software is free and open source under the MIT licence. The only costs are optional third-party ones you control: the voice agent uses your own OpenAI API credit (the app warns at $2 and caps at $5 per session), and photoreal 3D tiles can be metered if you use a direct Google key instead of the free Cesium ion route.
faqs.q: Is God's Eye View really free?

faqs.a: For practical purposes, no. Google Earth's imagery is archival — days to years old depending on the place — assembled for clarity, not freshness. God's Eye View is the live one of this pair: its flights, ships, satellites, earthquakes and cameras refresh from live public feeds.

Only God's Eye View: its CCTV Mesh layer states a shared cap of about 4,000 cameras, projected into its 3D scene. Google Earth has no live cameras — Street View is recorded imagery. For comparison, WorldEye's directory lists 74,229 public cameras.
faqs.q: Which has live cameras, God's Eye View or Google Earth?

faqs.a: No. Google Earth runs on the web and in iOS/Android apps; a Google account is optional, needed only for saving places and projects. God's Eye View is the opposite: no account at all, but you install it on your own computer first.
faqs.q: Do I need to install anything for Google Earth?

faqs.a: Google Earth, by a wide margin: its historical imagery reaches back decades for many places. God's Eye View has no general history scrubber — only specific timelines such as weather observations and launch replays.
faqs.q: Which is better for seeing how a place has changed over time?

intro: God's Eye View and Google Earth both put a photorealistic planet on your screen — and they are built for opposite moments. God's Eye View is free, open-source software (by Bilawal Sidhu and Sameh Khamis) that you install on your own computer: a live 3D globe with flights, ships, satellites, cameras and weather happening now, driven by voice. Google Earth is Google's hosted classic: the deepest archive of satellite and aerial imagery ever assembled, with 3D cities and Street View — a world as it was photographed, not as it is this minute.
pricingA: There is no God's Eye View price or subscription — the software is free and open source. The README's own cost table is honest about the edges: most layers cost $0 with no signup; a free-key tier (AISStream, NASA FIRMS, Cesium ion within quota) unlocks more; the voice agent spends your own OpenAI credit with a $2 warning and $5 hard cap per session; and photoreal tiles through a direct Google key are metered by Google.
pricingB: Completely free — Google Earth Pro (once $399/year) has been free since 2015. No paid tiers, no subscriptions; a Google account is optional.
prosA: Completely free and open source (MIT) — no subscription, ever
Live flights, ships, satellites, earthquakes and cameras on one 3D globe
Voice-controlled AI agent — talk to the globe
Runs locally: your data and keys stay on your machine
Endlessly extendable — every layer is a module
prosB: The most detailed 3D cities and terrain anywhere, permanently free
Street View puts you at ground level in place after place
Historical imagery archive reaching back decades
Measurement, drawing and KML/KMZ tools for serious place work
Nothing to install — web and mobile apps billions already know

verdictA: Choose God's Eye View if you want the planet as it is right now — live flights, ships, cameras and weather on a photoreal 3D globe you control by voice — and you're comfortable installing software to get it free and open forever.
verdictB: Choose Google Earth if you want the deepest, most detailed look at places as they were — historical imagery, 3D cities, Street View and mapping tools, free forever, with nothing to install.
verdictLine: God's Eye View is the present tense — a live, voice-driven 3D globe you own and can extend. Google Earth is the archive — the deepest record of how places looked, in 3D and at street level. The first is free software you install; the second is a free explorer you simply open.
worldEye: If installing software is the dealbreaker in God's Eye View, and Google Earth's archive can't show you anything live, WorldEye is the middle path: a hosted 3D globe that opens free in any browser with no signup at all — 74,229 public cameras across 109 countries, live flights, ships, satellites, weather, earthquakes and wildfires in the same view. It doesn't match Google Earth's 3D cities, Street View or decades-deep archive, or render photoreal 3D tiles like God's Eye View, and its Pro tier ($7.99/week, $13.99/month or $74.99/year) buys an OSINT toolkit and intel feeds rather than an imagery archive.
